en: When using Pi,
it's very important to understand that
unlike some other coding agents,
it has broad permissions
right out of the box. Now, actually, when
you start a Pi session, you may be greeted
with a trust screen like this
where you're asked whether you want to trust
this
project. And you can then either choose to
trust it, to trust the parent folder, or
only trust for this session, or not trust.
And this is required You need to trust it in
order for Pi and the agent
to be able to do meaningful work in there.
So that is one layer of protection you have.
But other than that, you have
none by default.
The coding agent can roam freely on your
system. Besides that trust setting, there is
no sandbox. And if it deletes something,
it's gone on your system. System.
There are no permission pop-ups whilst it's
working, as you may know it from other
coding agents. There's none of that. There
is only that trust setting. And as they
clearly mention on the official docs,
project trust only controls whether Pi loads
project local settings, resources, packages,
and extensions.
It is not a sandbox. So that trust setting
does not restrict what the model can ask
tools to do. It can still do anything, even
if you don't trust it. Only about loading
settings, project-specific settings,
resources, and packages. So it's only a
tiny, tiny little layer there. And in
general, and that's the philosophy of PyPI,
PyPI can do
anything, which makes it very powerful,
but it's also something to be aware of. And
you therefore may not want to run it if that
is not something you are fine with.
Now you can restrict it a bit though.
